title: Vaginal yeast infection (thrush)
intro: Vaginal thrush is a common infection caused by an overgrowth of Candida yeast, which normally lives in small numbers in the vagina. It causes itching, soreness and a thick white discharge. It is not a sexually transmitted infection and is easily treated with antifungal creams, pessaries or tablets.

sections.heading: Causes and triggers
paragraphs: Thrush happens when the balance of vaginal organisms is disturbed. Triggers include antibiotics, pregnancy, uncontrolled diabetes, a weakened immune system, hormonal changes, and sometimes irritating soaps, tight synthetic clothing or douching. Many women get it occasionally, and some have repeated episodes.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Typical symptoms are itching and irritation of the vagina and vulva, redness and swelling, burning when passing urine or during sex, and a thick, white, odourless discharge like cottage cheese. Similar symptoms can be caused by other conditions such as bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, skin conditions and allergies, so the first episode is best confirmed by a doctor.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Antifungal treatment is available as vaginal pessaries, creams or a single tablet taken by mouth. Most women improve within a few days and complete the course as directed. Antifungal cream applied to the vulva helps with external itching. Tablets are not recommended in pregnancy, so ask for local treatment. Do not use tampons or have sex until treated if it causes discomfort.

sections.heading: Recurrent thrush
paragraphs: Four or more episodes a year warrant medical review. Doctors may confirm the diagnosis with a swab, check for diabetes, and prescribe a longer course followed by preventive weekly treatment for several months. Identify possible triggers and review medicines.

sections.heading: Prevention
paragraphs: Wear breathable cotton underwear, avoid scented products and douching, wash with plain water or mild unscented cleanser, change out of wet swimwear or sweaty clothing promptly and control blood sugar if diabetic. Probiotics have uncertain benefit. Seek advice if symptoms do not improve within a week, or if there is fever, abdominal pain or foul-smelling discharge.

examples.title: Choosing treatment
examples.text: Imagine you have typical symptoms and a previous diagnosis. You could ask a pharmacist about an antifungal pessary or tablet and follow the full course.

examples.title: Dealing with frequent episodes
examples.text: Suppose you have thrush after each antibiotic course. You might discuss prevention with your doctor and note the pattern in a diary.

questions: Is this thrush, or could it be another infection?
